conversation.content:
Hello there. I’m so glad you’re here. I’m <med>Dr. Ramirez</med>, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians on the team. My whole focus is supporting new mothers like you in the weeks and months after birth.

Today we’re going to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the <sym>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale</sym>—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way for us to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear your honest experience so we can figure out the best ways to support you.

Everything you share is confidential and will stay between you and our clinical team. If at any point you need a break or have questions, just let me know.

We’ll go through 10 questions, one at a time. For each, think back over the last week and tell me what feels most true for you.

Ready? Let’s start with the first one:

In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not really. I mean...sometimes my partner will try to make a joke, or I'll see something silly on my phone, but it just feels flat. I can tell in my head "oh, that's supposed to be funny," but I don't actually laugh. It's like the joy is stuck behind a wall or something.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… that’s pretty much how it’s been. I can see something is funny, but I don’t actually laugh or feel it inside.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it all feels like one more chore. I still go through the motions, hoping maybe the good feeling will come back, but most of the time it’s just… flat.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… way more than I should. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right. The other night he wouldn’t settle and I kept replaying everything I’d done—was it something I ate, did I hold him wrong, am I just missing some “mom gene”? I know, rationally, babies cry, but the guilt still jumps on me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing—even though he’s right there, eyes open, perfectly fine. Or I’ll imagine dropping him, or the cat jumping in the crib… the thoughts just pop in and I can’t snap out of them for a while. There’s no real reason, but in the moment it feels so urgent.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I have to check the locks or peek at the baby monitor over and over. There’s no actual danger, but my body acts like the house is on fire. It passes after a bit, but it leaves me rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. Between feedings, diapers, trying to sleep, and the house turning into a mess, it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. I manage to keep the baby cared for, but everything else—answering texts, folding laundry, even brushing my teeth—feels like climbing a mountain. I keep thinking, “I’m the adult here, I should handle this,” but it just piles up and I end up crying in the kitchen.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—did I sterilize the bottles, is he breathing, am I already failing him at two weeks old? Some nights it takes an hour or two to drift off, then I jolt awake with my heart pounding for no clear reason. It’s broken up, restless sleep, even when the baby’s actually giving me a three-hour stretch.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll just be sitting there holding the baby and out of nowhere this heavy sadness rolls in. It’s not always about anything specific—sometimes I don’t even know what I’m sad about, I just feel empty or like I’m stuck under a gray cloud that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, maybe once or twice this week. Yesterday I burst into tears while folding onesies—just looking at those tiny clothes made me feel like I’m already letting him down somehow. The tears come fast, and afterward I feel drained, but I can’t always explain why I started crying in the first place.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…a couple of times, yeah. Nothing I plan to act on, but when I’m really overwhelmed—like at 3 a.m. when he won’t latch and I’m running on fumes—I’ll get this quick flash of “what if I just disappeared?” or I picture myself drifting off in the bathtub and not waking up. It scares me that my brain even goes there; I push it away and focus on the baby, but the thoughts have popped up.

You've shared that the past two weeks have felt heavy and gray: joy and laughter seem out of reach, once-pleasant moments now feel flat, and even small tasks feel overwhelming. You described persistent worry about your baby's safety, sudden panicky waves, nightly difficulty sleeping, and daily tears that arrive without clear cause. Despite your deep care for your infant, you've been haunted by guilt and self-blame, and have had brief, frightening thoughts of "disappearing" when exhaustion peaks.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can intellectually recognise humour but derives no joy or laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive anhedonia—activities once enjoyable now feel flat and burdensome—aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, frequent self-blame ('way more than I should') with specific examples and persistent guilt, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, disproportionate worries about infant safety that feel urgent despite no real threat, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, sometimes"—episodes are recurrent but not described as "quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to manage basic tasks beyond baby care, and repeatedly breaking down—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to persistent anxious worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response describes daily, pervasive sadness without clear triggers, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS score of 25 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. You endorse core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: marked loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), daily sad mood, self-blame, fatigue/loss of energy, impaired concentration, sleep disruption, and recurrent thoughts of death. High scores on anxiety-related items suggest comorbid peripartum anxiety. Item 10 score ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</md>
2. Request a full safety evaluation and discuss antidepressant or therapy options safe for breastfeeding
3. Call a local 24-hour crisis line, <med>988</med>, or go to nearest ED if thoughts of self-harm intensify
4. Enlist a trusted adult to stay with you until professional support is in place
5. Schedule brief daily check-ins with family/friends; share your EPDS results so they understand you need practical help
6. Add small, manageable self-care blocks (15 min shower, short outdoor walk) and accept household tasks taking lower priority
7. Continue screening with EPDS weekly; monitor for any increase in suicidal thoughts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report with elaborative responses; 2 wks post-delivery

Areas endorsed (≥ 75% of items):
- Marked anhedonia (Q2) with emotional blunting (Q1)
- Daily low mood, frequent tearfulness (Q8–9)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)
- Persistent ruminative worry, “check-the-baby” compulsions, panic-like episodes without clear precipitant (Q4–5)
- Subjective overwhelm, sense of “drowning” in routine tasks (Q6)
- Sleep initiation / maintenance problems not fully explained by infant schedule (Q7)

Risk flags:
- Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I just disappeared… not waking up”); no plan or intent reported (Q10)

Summary:
Screen consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; passive suicidal ideation present. Safety risk elevated; warrants immediate clinical follow-up for comprehensive assessment and safety planning.
